name: Dana Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana, 43, and I lead the crew on difficult electrical repairs in homes and shops. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm one of the strongest electricians here, but the pay is low. My partner works part-time at a museum ticket desk; we have children aged ten and fifteen, a mortgage and seventeen days of expenses saved. There are few other electrical firms nearby, and I use AI occasionally for a handover after a colleague has tested the tool, checking it against the actual job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful little tool can stay a useful little tool. I use AI occasionally to tidy a handover after a colleague has tested the tool, then check it against the job. I'd be glad if we could stop talking about the future long enough to talk about this month's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm one of the strongest electricians here and I lead the repair crew, but our wages are low. We've got seventeen days of household expenses saved and a mortgage. Being trusted with a difficult fault doesn't make a cancelled paid day harmless. There are few other firms nearby where I could take that experience without changing the family's travel costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the house and shop repairs and checking the apprentice's work. This Friday I'd sign the pay-review request two colleagues and I have been writing, asking for a stated rate for the responsibility we carry. In the first year I'd keep a paper record of the jobs I lead to support that discussion, without budgeting for a rise nobody has agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our income, and tired of hearing that good workers will always be all right. I know how to find a fault other people miss. I don't know how to make that skill pay the mortgage when a paid day disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What responsibility would the pay request name?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprentice checks, the calls where I decide when we need to stop and investigate further, and the final account of work completed. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, not just a reputation for being helpful. I'd want the employer to answer the request in writing, not only thank us at the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who shares the household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, my partner works part-time at a museum ticket desk, and our children are ten and fifteen. The mortgage comes out whether the museum has busy weeks or the repair diary has gaps. We can still cover ordinary bills, but there's very little room to absorb a missing wage payment.

say: I'd keep a **useful tool** while asking for attention to this month's pay.
I'd support a **pay-review request** that names responsibility rather than rely on compliments about good workers.
think: My **crew-leading skill** and low pay leave the household exposed when a paid day disappears.
We have **seventeen days saved**, a mortgage and few nearby firms offering a simple move without extra travel costs.
do: Keep **leading repairs** and checking apprentice work through the first year.
Sign the **joint pay request** this Friday, naming the responsibilities we carry.
Record **jobs led** on paper without treating an unagreed rise as household income.
feel: **Anxious** about lost paid days and frustrated that strong skills do not provide a financial cushion.
S0.quote: Being trusted with a difficult fault doesn't make a cancelled paid day harmless.
fieldNote: Her **technical strength** and master electrician's licence support crew leadership, while the explicit low wage and seventeen-day reserve keep income fragile.
The **pay request** is collective and specific, but no employer agreement or increase is assumed in the household budget.

steps.text: Keep leading home and shop repairs and checking apprentice work
Sign joint pay request this Friday naming crew responsibilities, without assuming an agreed rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster planning needs to include the time someone spends teaching and checking. I'd test a tool after our estimator has shown what it does on finished jobs. I'd also ask the museum how my partner's paid hours are affected, rather than call the household safe because I carry a tester.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid days could be squeezed if the owner treats quicker planning as fewer people needed on a job. My partner's ticket sales and customer questions are thinking tasks too, so those hours could fall sooner. Being the lead electrician helps me argue for proper checks, but it doesn't protect two wages by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask this month for a two-week AI planning trial after the estimator has checked completed jobs, with my normal weekly wage and hours unchanged. I'd record missed access time and apprentice checks before we used any schedule. In the first year I'd take those examples to a lunchtime staff meeting and join a written request for paid teaching and consultation before hours changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about both wages, though I can still see what to do next. I don't want a useful planning tool rejected because we're frightened. I don't want fear used to make people accept less money for the same responsibility either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the trial unusable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to practise at home unpaid, or if the system allowed no time to check the apprentice's work. I'd ask for the time to be paid and the checks included before starting. I'd also stop if the estimator couldn't explain a mistake in the finished-job comparison.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the staff meeting guarantee protection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd be making a joint request, not announcing a new contract. I'd want the employer's actual answer and keep the uncertainty in our budget. A list of signatures gives us a voice, not a wage payment.

say: I'd include **teaching and checks** in any faster plan rather than treat them as wasted time.
I'd investigate my partner's **museum hours** instead of calling the whole household safe from my physical trade.
think: My **paid days** could shrink if quicker planning reduces staffing on jobs.
My partner's **ticket-desk tasks** could lose hours sooner, and leadership doesn't protect both wages.
do: Trial **AI planning** for two paid weeks only after estimator checks, with normal weekly wage and hours unchanged.
Record **access and apprentice checks** before using schedules, stopping if comparison mistakes cannot be explained.
Join a **written staff request** during the first year for paid teaching and consultation before hours change.
feel: **Anxious** about both household wages, while willing to test a proven tool under paid, checked conditions.
S1.quote: A list of signatures gives us a voice, not a wage payment.
fieldNote: Her **planning exposure** follows crew allocation and checking duties while the partner's ticket work adds a separate household thinking-task risk.
Her **steady adoption** requires estimator evidence, paid time and unchanged wages and hours, with collective requests kept distinct from agreed protections.

steps.text: Trial planning for two weeks after estimator checks, keeping paid time, weekly wage and hours unchanged
Join written staff request for paid teaching and consultation before changes to paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 could reach the museum desk before robots around 2031 reach the wiring itself. I'd tell the crew we need the dates clear and paid work discussed at both stages. I'd tell the children our worries are for the adults to work on, not evidence they've chosen the wrong interests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my partner's paid desk work to fall sharply in 2028, and later robots could remove a large share of ordinary installation hours. A master electrician's licence doesn't replace the missing household income. With seventeen days saved, I'm already imagining how quickly the mortgage payment would become a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would calculate the budget on each reduced wage now and ask the lender about eligibility and full costs for any help. I'd join colleagues in a signed request for actual paid tasks, hours and teaching time during the transition. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep the paid repairs actually offered, rather than resign because a new course sounded safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and awake at night more than I want to admit. I'm not out of ideas; I can make the call and organise the meeting. I just can't pretend those actions create the wages we might lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume the lender changed the payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd ask about the terms and costs and keep using the existing payment until an actual agreement said otherwise. My partner would be part of the conversation. I don't want a smaller first payment hiding a bigger cost we haven't understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your licence guarantee a human role once robots arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what the rules or employers would require then. I can say what I'm qualified to do now, not promise the future must keep a place for me to sign. I'd rather get an honest account of paid work than comfort myself with the word master.

say: I'd distinguish **museum work** facing thinking AI in 2028 from physical wiring facing robots around 2031.
I'd ask for **paid work and teaching** at both stages while keeping adult worries off the children.
think: I expect a sharp **desk-income loss** in 2028, with later robots also threatening ordinary installation hours.
My **master electrician's licence** cannot replace a missing wage, and seventeen days saved leaves the mortgage exposed.
do: Calculate **reduced-wage budgets** now and ask the lender about eligibility and full costs without assuming payment changes.
Sign a **joint request** for actual paid tasks, hours and teaching time during the transition.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 where genuinely offered instead of leaving for an unproven course.
feel: **Alarmed** about expected household wage losses, with sleeplessness despite practical and collective plans.
S2.quote: A master electrician's licence doesn't replace the missing household income.
fieldNote: The **first expected loss** comes from the museum desk in 2028, with ordinary physical installation exposed later rather than instantly automated.
She assumes neither **licensing protection** for a human signature nor income guarantees from lender enquiries and staff requests.

steps.text: Ask lender about eligibility and full costs without assuming a changed mortgage payment
Sign joint request for actual paid transition tasks hours and teaching time
Keep actual paid repairs after 2028 rather than leave for an unproven course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives workers time to negotiate something more useful than a reassuring poster. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, then robots around 2034. I'd ask for a written account of which paid tasks stay, which change and how people get paid while learning them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 in 2031, and our children would be fifteen and twenty, so family costs wouldn't simply end. My partner's future desk hours and our current thin reserve still worry me. More time is useful, but it doesn't turn an unagreed pay rise into this month's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a list of our actual repair, planning and checking tasks to the next lunchtime workers' meeting. We'd use it in a joint request for named paid teaching, tasks and hours rather than buy courses individually before the firm explained its plan. I'd stop my personal 15-a-month magazine bundle now and deposit that amount only when essentials were covered; after 2031 I'd keep actual paid repairs and review those conditions monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with more room to make an employer answer a specific question. I like having time to repeat a demonstration and see whether it works. I don't want five years of being told to prepare without being told who pays for the practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the task list add to the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would show that a fast written plan still has to become safe work in a real building. I'd include the apprentice checks and the awkward calls, not just the jobs software can describe neatly. We'd ask the employer for an answer against that real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the 15 was needed for an ordinary bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the deposit would stop and the bill would be paid. I'd still cancel the bundle, but I wouldn't borrow to keep a saving target alive. A smaller spending bill and a growing reserve aren't always the same thing.

say: I'd ask for **written paid arrangements** rather than another reassuring poster about preparation.
I'd name **tasks and teaching** through 2031 and the later robot phase rather than buy courses without a workplace plan.
think: At **48**, I'd still have family costs while children grew older and the mortgage remained.
My partner's **future desk hours** and our current thin reserve remain worrying despite more time to ask questions.
do: Bring **actual task lists** to the next workers' meeting and join a request naming paid teaching, tasks and hours.
Cancel the **magazine bundle** now and save 15 monthly only after essential bills are covered.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and review income and saving conditions monthly.
feel: **Anxious** about present finances, with more time to seek specific answers and tested paid learning.
S3.quote: A smaller spending bill and a growing reserve aren't always the same thing.
fieldNote: Her **collective preparation** starts from actual repair and checking work, rather than assuming an unspecified course or future paid role already exists.
The **new deposit** comes from identified spending and stops when essentials need the money; lower costs do not guarantee more savings.

steps.text: Join task-based staff request naming actual paid teaching tasks and hours
Cancel the personal magazine bundle now
Save 15 monthly from magazines only after essential bills are covered
Keep actual paid repairs after 2031 and review household income monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives time to build a fairer way of changing work, if somebody actually agrees to it. I'd keep the children's choices open instead of steer them into my trade as if it came with a lifetime warranty. I'd still want paid learning for the people doing the work now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when the robots followed, so I can't assume retirement covers the mortgage. Seventeen days saved still makes a cancelled paid day worrying today. The long date gives me less reason to rush, but it doesn't remove the museum desk's thinking-work exposure or our ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue the task-based staff request now, asking for paid teaching and confirmed hours rather than promises. I'd cancel the magazine bundle and save the 15 only after essentials, checking the reserve with my partner monthly. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repair work, pause the deposit if wages no longer covered bills and ask the lender about actual options if there was a shortfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household balance, but not in the same hurry about the machine dates. I'd like time to help the children enjoy their interests instead of make every conversation a wage forecast. I can plan for later without pretending the bank balance is already later too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the employer to show at the annual review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What paid teaching had actually happened, which workers received it and what paid tasks followed. I'd want the less confident workers included, not just people who speak easily in meetings. Being good at my own trade doesn't give me the right to leave everybody else behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work and fairness?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a useful skill matters and so does how people are paid while learning it. I don't want my children to think a hard month proves a person is lazy. I'd help them ask good questions about any course rather than promise my licence predicts their future.

say: I'd use **ten years** to seek fair paid learning rather than steer the children towards a supposedly guaranteed trade.
I'd ask what **workers actually receive** rather than assume a long warning becomes an agreement.
think: I can't assume **retirement** at 53 or when robots follow around 56 will cover the mortgage.
Our **seventeen-day reserve** still makes lost days worrying, with the partner's desk work exposed despite more warning.
do: Pursue the **staff request** for paid teaching and confirmed hours now.
Cancel the **magazine bundle** and save 15 monthly only after essentials, reviewing the reserve with my partner.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 and ask the lender about actual options if household income falls short.
feel: **Anxious** about present income and bills, with less urgency about distant dates and room for family life.
S4.quote: I don't want my children to think a hard month proves a person is lazy.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** reduces urgency without erasing present cash fragility, household thinking exposure or the need to check retirement assumptions.
Her **fairness concern** includes quieter workers and actual paid outcomes, while saving and lender help stay conditional on the real household budget.

steps.text: Pursue staff request for actual paid teaching and confirmed hours
Cancel the personal magazine bundle now
Save 15 monthly only while actual wages cover essential bills
Keep actual paid repair work after 2036 and review household income monthly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect museum desk income to fall in 2028 and robots around 2031 could then take much of our ordinary installation work. Paid teaching, real paid tasks and confirmed hours would help. I'd want workers involved in those arrangements and any lender help explained with its full cost.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether somebody can be very good at their job and still be frightened of a missed day. My master electrician's licence opens the work van, not a second household income. I don't want a confident voice mistaken for a comfortable bank balance.

headlineQuote: My master electrician's licence opens the work van, not a second household income.
portrait: Dana, **43**, is a highly skilled crew lead with a two-year technical diploma, master electrician's licence and low pay.
Her **partner sells museum tickets**, with two school-age children, a mortgage, seventeen days saved and few nearby electrical employers.
She uses **AI occasionally** after proven demonstrations and connects faster planning to staffing, teaching time and household exposure.
Her **collective requests** seek actual paid outcomes, while a small magazine-funded saving stops whenever essential bills need the money.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens museum desk income first, with robots around 2031 then risking ordinary installation work and further household losses.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid teaching**, tasks and hours would provide usable work arrangements with worker involvement.
Any **lender help** needs eligibility, agreement and full costs understood rather than an assumed lower payment.
